question: How did Jesus cure the blind man?
summary: Mark 8:22-25 has Jesus heal a blind man at Bethsaida by spitting directly on his eyes and laying hands on him — twice, because the first attempt only half-worked. John 9:1-7 has Jesus heal a blind man in Jerusalem by spitting on the ground, mixing clay, anointing the man's eyes, and sending him to wash in the Pool of Siloam. Different cities, different methods, different timeline, and a different number of steps. Apologists treat them as separate events; the literary parallels suggest John has reworked the Markan tradition into something more dignified.

reconcile.connective: Clarke treats the spittle in each account as a natural preliminary — separating the eyelids — not the miracle itself, which came through touch.

discrepancy.connective: D. F. Strauss argued John's man-born-blind story is a legendary 'heightening' of the Synoptic blind-healing tradition, shaped by the Fourth Gospel's dogmatic aims.

skeptic.name: D. F. Strauss
skeptic.work: The Life of Jesus Critically Examined

pd_work.author: Adam Clarke
pd_work.note: Clarke's note on Mark 8:23 is keyed to this exact passage and explicitly cross-references John 9:6, arguing the spittle in each account served a preparatory, non-miraculous purpose distinct from the healing act itself (used here in place of Haley, whose 1874 work has no indexed entry for 'Siloam,' 'spittle,' or 'born blind' and appears not to treat this specific comparison).

excerpts.attribution: Adam Clarke, Commentary on the Bible (1832)
excerpts.excerpt_text: There is a similar transaction to this mentioned by John, Joh 9:6. It is likely this was done merely to separate the eyelids; as, in certain cases of blindness, they are found always gummed together. It required a miracle to restore the sight, and this was done in consequence of Christ having laid his hands upon the blind man: it required no miracle to separate the eyelids, and, therefore, natural means only were employed - this was done by rubbing them with spittle; but whether by Christ, or by the blind man, is not absolutely certain.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Clarke explicitly cross-references John 9:6 from within his Mark 8:23 note and offers a functional distinction (spittle = natural prep, touch = the miracle) that speaks directly to why the reported 'methods' differ.
excerpts.source_note_text:
And he took the blind man by the hand - Giving him a proof of his readiness to help him, and thus preparing him for the cure which he was about to work.
Led him out of the town - Thus showing the inhabitants that he considered them unworthy of having another miracle wrought among them. He had already deeply deplored their ingratitude and obstinacy: see on Mat 11:21 (note). When a people do not make a proper improvement of the light and grace which they receive from God, their candlestick is removed - even the visible Church becomes there extinct; and the candle is put out - no more means of spiritual illumination are afforded to the unfaithful inhabitants: Rev 2:5.
When he had spit on his eyes - There is a similar transaction to this mentioned by John, Joh 9:6. It is likely this was done merely to separate the eyelids; as, in certain cases of blindness, they are found always gummed together. It required a miracle to restore the sight, and this was done in consequence of Christ having laid his hands upon the blind man: it required no miracle to separate the eyelids, and, therefore, natural means only were employed - this was done by rubbing them with spittle; but whether by Christ, or by the blind man, is not absolutely certain. See on Mar 7:33 (note). It has always been evident that false miracles have been wrought without reason or necessity, and without any obvious advantage; and they have thereby been detected: on the contrary, true miracles have always vindicated themselves by their obvious utility and importance; nothing ever being effected by them that could be performed by natural means.
If he saw aught - Ει, if, is wanting in the Syriac, all the Persic and Arabic, and in the Ethiopic; and τι βλεπεις, Dost thou see any thing? is the reading of CD, Coptic, Ethiopic, all the Arabic and Persic.
